title: Modules & Packages
intro: Module bugs are some of the most confusing in Node: a value that is undefined only at startup, a package that works with import but not require, or a build that differs between laptops and CI. Interviewers ask about modules and npm to see if you understand how code is actually loaded and how you keep the dependency tree reproducible and safe.

questions.title: CommonJS vs ES modules
questions.question: What are the real differences between CommonJS and ES modules in Node, beyond the syntax?
questions.short: CommonJS uses `require`/`module.exports`, loads synchronously, and runs code as it is required, so `require` can be called anywhere. ES modules use `import`/`export`, are parsed and linked before any code runs, are always in strict mode, support top-level await, and give live bindings: an import is a read-only view of the exporter variable, not a copy. ESM has no `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` or `__dirname`, and `this` at the top level is undefined instead of `module.exports`.
questions.simple: CommonJS hands you a photocopy of the notes at the moment you ask. ESM gives you a window into the other person's notebook, so you always see the latest value, but you cannot write in it.

head: CommonJS
ES modules
rows: Parse + link the whole graph first, then evaluate; can be async
Static imports at top level; `import()` for dynamic
You get the value of `module.exports` (objects by reference, primitives copied when you destructure)

explain.p: Because ESM imports and exports are known before any code runs, bundlers can tree-shake unused exports, and Node can report a missing named export as a `SyntaxError` before running anything. With CommonJS, `module.exports` is just an object built at runtime.

explain.note: Importing JSON directly in ESM uses import attributes: `import pkg from "./package.json" with { type: "json" }`. The older `assert { type: "json" }` form was removed in Node 22.

anim.title: Live binding (ESM) vs copied value (CJS)

steps.note: ESM: the module exports the variable count itself, not its current value.
The import creates a binding that points to the same variable in counter.mjs.
inc() changes the variable inside counter.mjs.
Reading count in main follows the binding, so we see 1. That is a live binding.
CommonJS: module.exports is a plain object. Its count property gets the value 0 copied in when the object is created.
Destructuring copies the number 0 into a new local variable in main.
inc() updates the local variable inside counter.cjs. Neither exports.count nor our copy changes.
We print our copy, so we get 0. To see updates in CJS you must export a getter or a function.

followups.q: Which should a new project use?
followups.a: ESM for new code, since it is the JavaScript standard and works the same in browsers and Node. CommonJS is still fine and very common in existing services; mixing needs care.

followups.q: Is ESM slower to start?
followups.a: ESM loading is async and does more work up front (linking), but in practice the difference is small. The bigger impact is usually the number of files, not the module system.

followups.q: Can you conditionally import in ESM?
followups.a: Use dynamic `await import("./x.js")`. It returns a promise of the module namespace and works in both ESM and CommonJS.

mistakes: Saying ESM imports are copies, or that CommonJS exports are live.
Forgetting the .js extension in relative ESM imports.
Expecting __dirname to exist in an .mjs file.

questions.title: How require() works
questions.question: Walk me through what happens when you call require("./user-service").
questions.short: Node first resolves the specifier to an absolute filename: core modules first, then relative or absolute paths trying the exact name, then `.js`, `.json`, `.node`, then a folder with package.json `main` or `index.js`; bare names walk up `node_modules` folders. It then checks `require.cache` by that filename and returns the cached `module.exports` if present. If not, it creates a Module object, caches it, wraps the source in a function `(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname)`, runs it synchronously, and returns `module.exports`.
questions.simple: require is a librarian: it finds the right shelf, and if the book is already on the desk it hands you that same copy. Only the first time does it actually go and read the book.

list: Built-in modules (`fs`, or `node:fs`, which always means the built-in) win.
`./` or `../` or `/`: try the path as is, then with `.js`, `.json`, `.node`. If it is a folder, use its package.json `main`, then `index.js`.
Bare names like `express`: look in `./node_modules`, then `../node_modules`, up to the root. If the package has an `"exports"` field, only the paths it lists can be loaded.
You can see the result with `require.resolve("x")` without loading it.

explain.p: `require.cache` is an object keyed by absolute filename. A hit returns the existing `module.exports` immediately. This is why a module body runs only once and why modules act like singletons.

explain.caption: The module wrapper. It is why these five names exist and why top-level variables are private to the file.

explain.p: The module is put in the cache before its code runs. That detail is what makes circular dependencies return a partially filled object instead of looping forever.

`exports` starts as a reference to `module.exports`. Adding properties to `exports` works, but `exports = {...}` only reassigns the local parameter and exports nothing. Use `module.exports = {...}` to replace the whole object.

list: Singletons: a DB pool created at module top level is shared by every file that requires it.
Two copies of the same package at different paths (for example two versions in node_modules) are two separate modules with separate state.
The cache key is the resolved path, so on case-insensitive file systems `./User` and `./user` can load the same file twice.
Deleting from `require.cache` forces a reload, but other modules still hold references to the old exports. It is mostly a test or hot-reload trick.

explain.note: JSON files are parsed and cached too, so `require("./config.json")` returns the same object every time. If you mutate it, every user sees the change.

anim.title: The module cache in action

steps.note: Built-in modules like fs come from Node itself. They are not stored as files in require.cache.
For the demo we write a small module file to the temp folder. It logs when its body runs and keeps a counter n.
First require: the path is resolved, there is no cache entry, so Node creates a Module, adds it to the cache, wraps the code and runs it.
The body finished. a now points to module.exports of counter.js.
Second require: cache hit. The body does not run again, so no second 'loading counter' line.
a and b are the same object and share the same n, so the counts go 1 then 2.
We delete the cache entry. The old module object still exists because a and b reference it.
require now misses the cache, so the body runs again and creates a fresh n.
c is a different object with its own counter, so c !== a and its first inc() returns 1.

followups.q: Why does `exports = { a: 1 }` not work?
followups.a: `exports` is just a parameter that initially points to `module.exports`. Reassigning it breaks that link, and require returns `module.exports`, which is still the original empty object.

followups.q: Is require synchronous even for big files?
followups.a: Yes. It reads and runs the file on the main thread. That is fine at startup but you should not call require for the first time inside hot request paths.

followups.q: How do ES modules cache?
followups.a: ESM has its own module map keyed by URL. It is not exposed like require.cache and you cannot delete entries; a different URL (for example a query string) creates a new instance.

mistakes: Reassigning `exports` instead of `module.exports`.
Assuming a module body runs every time it is required.
Expecting two versions of a package in node_modules to share state.

questions.title: Circular dependencies
questions.question: What happens with circular dependencies in CommonJS and in ES modules?
questions.short: In CommonJS, when a.js requires b.js and b.js requires a.js back, b gets a's exports object as it is at that moment, partially filled, because a is cached before it finishes running. No error, just possibly missing properties, and if a later replaces module.exports, b keeps the old object. In ESM the bindings are linked first, so b can import from a, but reading a binding that a has not initialised yet throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone); hoisted function declarations do work.
questions.simple: Two people each need the other's finished homework to start. CommonJS lets one copy the other's half-done page. ESM gives a link to the page but shouts if you read a line that has not been written yet.

explain.p: Node does not loop forever because a.js is already in `require.cache`. b.js gets that unfinished module. Node prints a warning if you read a property that does not exist on a module in a circular dependency.

list: Move the shared piece into a third module that both import.
Require or use the dependency lazily, inside a function that runs later, not at module top level.
Use dependency injection: pass the dependency in instead of importing it.
Find cycles with tools like `madge --circular`.

explain.note: Cycles that only use each other inside functions called later usually work in both systems. The problems come from using the other module at load time.

anim.title: CommonJS cycle: b sees a half-finished a

steps.note: main requires a.js. It is not cached, so Node caches an empty exports object for a and starts running a.
a sets loaded = false on its exports.
a requires b.js. b is new, so it is cached and starts running. a is paused in the middle.
b sets its own loaded = false.
b requires a.js. a is already in the cache, so Node returns it immediately, even though a has not finished. No infinite loop.
b sees the half-finished a, so a.loaded is still false.
b finishes and sets loaded = true. Control returns to a.
a sees the complete b.
a finishes. Because b kept a reference to the same exports object, b would now also see a.loaded = true if it read it later.
main gets the finished a.

followups.q: Why does reading a property later work but at load time not?
followups.a: b holds a reference to the same exports object. By the time a function in b runs later, a has finished filling that object. Only reads during loading see the partial state.

followups.q: How do you detect cycles in a large codebase?
followups.a: Run a dependency graph tool like madge or dependency-cruiser in CI, and watch for the Node warning about accessing properties inside a circular dependency.

mistakes: Saying Node throws an error for circular requires in CommonJS.
Replacing module.exports after a cycle has already handed out the old object.
Assuming ESM makes cycles safe; it turns silent undefined into a ReferenceError.

questions.title: "type", .mjs/.cjs and "exports"
questions.question: How does Node decide whether a file is ESM or CommonJS? And what does the "exports" field in package.json do?
questions.short: `.mjs` is always ESM and `.cjs` is always CommonJS. A `.js` file follows the nearest package.json: `"type": "module"` means ESM, `"type": "commonjs"` or no field means CommonJS. The `exports` field defines the public entry points of a package: only listed paths can be imported, which hides internals, and conditional exports let you point `import` and `require` (and other conditions like `types` or `node`) to different files.
questions.simple: The "type" field is the house rule for which language .js files speak; .mjs and .cjs carry their own passports. "exports" is the front desk: visitors can only go to the rooms it lists.

explain.p: Since Node 22.7 (and 20.19), Node can also detect ESM syntax in an ambiguous `.js` file with no type field and load it as ESM. Do not rely on it: set `"type"` explicitly so tools and humans know.

list: Encapsulation: `import "@acme/sdk/dist/internal.js"` fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`. You can refactor internal files freely.
Subpaths: `@acme/sdk/errors` maps to a real file.
Conditions are checked in object order; the first match wins. Put `types` first and `default` last.
Common conditions: `import`, `require`, `node`, `default`, plus community ones like `types`, `browser`, `development`.
When `exports` exists, it wins over `main` for Node versions that support it.

explain.p: Shipping both ESM and CJS builds means an app can load both copies: one via import, one via require. They are separate module instances, so `instanceof` checks fail and singletons are duplicated. Mitigations: keep state in one shared CJS file, ship only one format, or (in newer Node) ship ESM only and let CJS users `require()` it.

explain.note: Adding an `exports` field to an existing package is a breaking change, because deep imports that used to work stop working.

followups.q: What is the "imports" field?
followups.a: Private, package-internal aliases that start with #, e.g. `"imports": { "#db": "./src/db/index.js" }`, so you can write `import db from "#db"` inside the package.

followups.q: Does TypeScript understand exports?
followups.a: Yes, with `moduleResolution` set to `node16`, `nodenext` or `bundler`. It reads the `types` condition.

mistakes: Putting the "default" condition before "import" or "require", so it always wins.
Forgetting that "type": "module" changes how every .js file in the package is loaded, including config files.
Adding "exports" in a minor release and breaking deep imports.

questions.title: ESM and CommonJS interop
questions.question: Can ES modules import CommonJS, and can CommonJS require ES modules? What are the limits?
questions.short: ESM can import CommonJS: the default import is `module.exports`, and Node tries to detect named exports with a static analyser, which works for simple `exports.x = ...` patterns. CommonJS loading ESM traditionally needs dynamic `import()`, which returns a promise. Newer Node supports `require()` of an ES module synchronously: unflagged in Node 22.12+ and 20.19+, and only if the ES module graph has no top-level await; otherwise it throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`.
questions.simple: ESM can always borrow from CommonJS. CommonJS used to have to send a letter and wait (import()); now in recent Node it can just walk over and take it, as long as the ESM side is not still waiting on something.

explain.p: Named exports come from a static scan (cjs-module-lexer). Patterns like `exports.greet = ...` or a shorthand object `module.exports = { greet }` are usually detected; object literals with inline values (`{ greet: (n) => ... }`) and exports built dynamically (in a loop, through a helper) are not. If a named import fails, fall back to the default import and destructure.

list: `require(esm)` returns the namespace object, so a default export is under `.default`.
If the ES module or any of its imports uses top-level await, `require()` throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`. Use `import()` instead.
On older versions `require()` of ESM throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`. This is why many CLI tools broke when popular packages went ESM-only.
Some versions print an ExperimentalWarning when this feature is used.
Library authors: if you can drop old Node versions, ESM-only is becoming realistic because CJS consumers on modern Node can require it.
App authors on CJS: pin the CommonJS-compatible major version of an ESM-only dependency, use `import()`, or migrate to ESM.
Check your minimum Node version before relying on require(esm).

explain.note: `import()` works in CommonJS too, which makes it the most portable bridge.

followups.q: What does __esModule mean?
followups.a: A flag set by transpilers like Babel and TypeScript on CJS output so that other transpiled code treats `exports.default` as the default export. Node itself ignores it when importing CJS from real ESM, so you can end up with `mod.default.default`.

followups.q: Why can't require handle top-level await?
followups.a: require must return synchronously. A module with top-level await cannot finish evaluating synchronously, so there is no value to return yet.

mistakes: Claiming require() can never load ESM; that is outdated for Node 22.12+ and 20.19+.
Claiming require(esm) works on every Node 20 or 22 release, or with top-level await.
Expecting named imports from every CommonJS package to work.

questions.title: package.json fields that matter
questions.question: Which package.json fields do you care about in a production service or a published library?
questions.short: For a service: `name`, `private: true` to prevent accidental publishing, `type`, `scripts`, `engines` for the Node version, `dependencies` and `devDependencies`, and sometimes `overrides` to force a patched transitive version and `packageManager`. For a library also `version`, `exports` (or `main`), `types`, `files` to control what gets published, `bin` for CLIs, `peerDependencies`, `license` and `sideEffects` for bundlers.
questions.simple: package.json is the ID card and instruction sheet for your project: who it is, what it needs, and how to run it.

head: Field
Why it matters
rows: npm refuses to publish it. Use for apps.
How `.js` files are loaded (ESM or CJS).
Documents the Node version; npm warns (or fails with `engine-strict`) on mismatch.
Entry points when someone imports the package.
Allow-list of what goes into the published tarball. Check with `npm pack --dry-run`.
Force a version of a transitive dependency (npm 8.3+). Yarn uses `resolutions`.

explain.note: Scripts run with `node_modules/.bin` on the PATH, so `"lint": "eslint ."` uses the local eslint without npx.
`--env-file` (Node 20.6+) loads a .env file without the dotenv package, and `--watch` restarts on changes.

followups.q: What is the "files" field vs .npmignore?
followups.a: `files` is an allow-list and is safer: only what you list (plus package.json, README, LICENSE) is published. .npmignore is a deny-list and it is easy to leak secrets or test fixtures.

followups.q: Do lifecycle scripts like postinstall run for dependencies?
followups.a: Yes, by default npm runs install scripts of all dependencies, which is a supply-chain risk. `--ignore-scripts` disables them.

mistakes: Not setting private: true on an application.
Publishing a library without "files", shipping tests or .env files.
Using engines but never enforcing it in CI.

questions.title: package-lock.json and npm ci
questions.question: What is package-lock.json for, and why should CI use npm ci instead of npm install?
questions.short: package.json lists version ranges; package-lock.json records the exact version, download URL and integrity hash of every package in the tree, so every machine installs the same thing. `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says, deletes any existing node_modules first, fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree, and never modifies the lockfile. `npm install` can resolve newer versions within the ranges and rewrite the lockfile, so it is for development, not for reproducible builds.
questions.simple: package.json is a shopping list that says "some milk". The lockfile is the receipt that says exactly which brand and size you bought, so everyone can buy the very same thing.

list: Exact version of every direct and transitive dependency.
The tarball URL and a sha512 integrity hash, so a tampered package fails to install.
The tree shape (which package is hoisted where).

head: npm install
npm ci
rows: package.json, uses lockfile as a guide
Lockfile is the source of truth

explain.code:
# Dockerfile (production deps only)
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

list: Commit package-lock.json for applications. For libraries it is also useful for your own CI, though consumers do not use your lockfile.
Review lockfile diffs in PRs: unexpected new packages or changed `resolved` URLs are red flags.
Resolve lockfile merge conflicts by regenerating with `npm install`, not by hand-editing.
Use one package manager per repo; pnpm and yarn have their own lockfiles.

anim.title: From install on a laptop to a reproducible CI build
anim.code:
# developer laptop
npm install express@^4.19.0
git add package.json package-lock.json
# CI server
npm ci
npm test

steps.note: npm install records the range ^4.19.0 in package.json. It is a rule, not a version.
npm asks the registry for the newest version matching the range, say 4.21.1, plus all its dependencies.
Packages are downloaded, hashes are checked, and node_modules is filled.
Both files are committed. The lockfile is what makes the next install repeatable.
Weeks later express 4.22.0 is out. On CI, npm ci ignores that: it first checks that the lockfile matches package.json.
It deletes any node_modules and installs exactly the locked versions, verifying each integrity hash.
Tests run against the same tree the developer had. npm install here might have picked 4.22.0 and rewritten the lockfile.

followups.q: Does a library's lockfile affect its users?
followups.a: No. npm ignores package-lock.json inside dependencies. Users resolve your ranges themselves. (npm-shrinkwrap.json is the exception, and is rarely appropriate for libraries.)

followups.q: How do you update a single dependency safely?
followups.a: Use `npm install pkg@version` or `npm update pkg`, run tests, and review the lockfile diff. Tools like Renovate or Dependabot automate this with small PRs.

mistakes: Using npm install in CI and getting different versions than developers tested.
Adding package-lock.json to .gitignore.
Hand-editing lockfile conflicts.

questions.title: Semver: ^ vs ~
questions.question: Explain semantic versioning. What do ^ and ~ mean in a dependency range?
questions.short: Semver is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major for breaking changes, minor for new backwards-compatible features, patch for bug fixes. `^1.4.2` allows anything from 1.4.2 up to but not including 2.0.0, so new minors and patches. `~1.4.2` allows only patches, from 1.4.2 up to 1.5.0. For 0.x versions caret is stricter: `^0.4.2` means up to 0.5.0, because in 0.x a minor bump may break things.
questions.simple: Caret says "any newer version that promises not to break me". Tilde says "only bug fixes, please".

explain.p: npm uses `^` by default when you `npm install pkg`. Combined with a lockfile, that is a good balance: ranges say what is compatible, the lockfile says what is actually installed.
`2.0.0-beta.1` is lower than `2.0.0`. Ranges do not match pre-releases unless the range itself names a pre-release with the same major.minor.patch, so `^1.0.0` never picks up `2.0.0-beta.1`.

explain.h: Semver is a promise, not a guarantee

list: Maintainers sometimes ship breaking changes in minors by accident.
That is why the lockfile and tests matter more than the range.
Some teams pin exact versions (`save-exact=true` in .npmrc) and let a bot propose updates.

explain.note: Check what a range resolves to with `npm view express@"^4.19.0" version` or experiment with the semver calculator from npm.

anim.title: Which versions does each range accept?

steps.note: Caret on a 1.0+ version: keep the major the same, allow newer minors and patches.
Candidate versions are checked. 4.19.3 and 4.21.1 match. 4.19.1 is too old and 5.0.0 is a new major.
Tilde: keep major and minor, allow only patch updates.
4.17.21 is a patch, so it is fine. 4.18.0 would be a new minor and is rejected.
Caret on a 0.x version is stricter: the first non-zero part is treated like the major.
0.4.9 is accepted, but 0.5.0 is rejected because in 0.x a minor bump may break the API.
npm installs the highest accepted version and writes it to the lockfile. Later installs with npm ci use the lockfile, not these ranges.

followups.q: Should you pin exact versions?
followups.a: For apps, the lockfile already pins everything, so ranges mostly affect updates. Pinning in package.json makes updates explicit and works well with an update bot. For libraries, use ranges so users can deduplicate.

followups.q: What does npm outdated show?
followups.a: For each dependency: the current installed version, the "wanted" version (highest within your range) and the "latest" published version.

mistakes: Thinking ^0.4.2 allows 0.9.0.
Thinking the range alone controls what CI installs, ignoring the lockfile.
Using * or latest for production dependencies.

questions.title: dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies
questions.question: What is the difference between dependencies, devDependencies and peerDependencies?
questions.short: `dependencies` are needed at runtime and are installed for anyone who installs your package. `devDependencies` are only for developing and building, like test runners, linters and TypeScript; they are skipped with `npm ci --omit=dev` and not installed for your package's users. `peerDependencies` say "I need this package, but the host app must provide it", typically for plugins like a React component library or an Express middleware with a specific major version. npm 7+ installs peers automatically and errors with ERESOLVE on conflicts.
questions.simple: dependencies are the ingredients in the dish. devDependencies are the kitchen tools. peerDependencies are "serve with rice", where the guest brings the rice.

head: Type
Installed for your users?
Installed in prod image?
Example
rows: Expected from the host app (npm 7+ auto-installs)
react for a UI kit, eslint for a plugin

explain.p: A plugin should use the same instance of its host as the app. If an ESLint plugin listed eslint in `dependencies`, the app could end up with two copies, and the plugin would register with the wrong one. A peer dependency says "share the app's copy, and it must be in this version range".

explain.caption: A plugin lists the host as a peer and also as a devDependency for its own tests.

explain.p: In a TypeScript service, `typescript` and `@types/*` belong in devDependencies if you compile in a build stage, but anything imported at runtime (even indirectly) must be in dependencies, or the production image built with `--omit=dev` crashes with "Cannot find module".

explain.note: `--legacy-peer-deps` makes npm ignore peer conflicts like npm 6 did. It unblocks installs but can hide real incompatibilities.

followups.q: What does ERESOLVE mean?
followups.a: npm could not build a tree that satisfies every peer dependency range, for example a plugin wants react 18 and the app has react 19. Fix the versions, use `overrides`, or as a last resort `--legacy-peer-deps`.

followups.q: Where do @types packages go?
followups.a: Usually devDependencies for apps. For a published TS library whose public types reference them, put them in dependencies so users get them.

mistakes: Putting runtime packages in devDependencies and crashing after npm ci --omit=dev.
Listing a framework as a regular dependency in a plugin, causing duplicate instances.
Using --legacy-peer-deps by default for every install.

questions.title: npx and npm exec
questions.question: What does npx do, and what should you be careful about?
questions.short: npx runs a package binary. It first looks in the local `node_modules/.bin`, then among globally installed npm packages; if the command is not found it downloads the package into the npm cache temporarily and runs it, asking for confirmation first in npm 7+. It is great for one-off tools and project-local CLIs, but downloading and running a package by name is a supply-chain risk: a typo can run a malicious package, so pin versions and prefer locally installed tools in scripts and CI.
questions.simple: npx is "use the tool from my toolbox, and if I do not have it, borrow one from the store just for this job". Borrowing from the store means you trust whatever is on that shelf.

explain.code:
npx eslint .                       # uses ./node_modules/.bin/eslint if installed
npx create-vite@5.5.2 my-app       # downloads that exact version and runs it
npx --yes prisma@5.20.0 generate   # skip the prompt (CI) - pin the version!
npm exec -- tsc --noEmit           # npm exec is the same engine as npx

list: Local project bins in `node_modules/.bin` (walking up the folders).
Bins of globally installed npm packages (`npm install -g`).
Otherwise, install the package into the npm cache (not your project) and run its bin.
With `-p` / `--package` you choose which package provides the command: `npx -p @angular/cli ng new app`.
Always pin a version for downloaded tools: `npx pkg@1.2.3`, not `npx pkg`.
Watch for typos: `npx create-reat-app` could be someone else's package.
In CI, prefer tools listed in devDependencies (locked by the lockfile) and run them through npm scripts.
A downloaded package's install scripts run on your machine.

explain.note: Inside npm scripts you do not need npx at all; `node_modules/.bin` is already on the PATH.

steps.note: npx first looks for eslint in the project node_modules/.bin. It is a devDependency, so it is there.
The local, lockfile-pinned eslint runs. Nothing is downloaded.
For create-vite, the local bin folder has nothing.
It is not installed globally either.
npm 7+ asks before installing an unknown package (unless --yes). This prompt is your last chance to spot a typo.
The pinned version is downloaded into the npm cache, not into your project, with its own dependencies.
Its bin runs with your arguments. Next time, the cached copy is reused.

followups.q: Difference between npx and npm run?
followups.a: npm run executes a named script from package.json. npx executes a package binary directly, installing it temporarily if needed.

followups.q: How do you run a different Node version for one command?
followups.a: With a version manager (nvm, fnm, volta), or `npx -p node@20 node script.js`, which downloads a Node binary package. Version managers are the cleaner choice.

mistakes: Using npx without a version in CI, so the tool changes under you.
Using npx inside npm scripts where it is unnecessary.
Assuming npx installs into the project.

questions.title: Dependency security
questions.question: How do you keep the dependencies of a Node service secure?
questions.short: I commit the lockfile and install with `npm ci` so builds are reproducible and integrity hashes are checked. I run `npm audit` (or Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk) in CI and fix high-severity issues that are actually reachable, using `overrides` for vulnerable transitive packages when needed. Against supply-chain attacks I keep the dependency count low, review new packages before adding them, pin versions for npx and CI tools, consider `--ignore-scripts`, use `npm audit signatures` to check registry signatures, and give the CI token and the running service the least privilege possible.
questions.simple: Your dependencies are strangers you let into your kitchen. You check their ID (lockfile and hashes), listen to alerts about known bad cooks (audit), and you do not let in more people than you need.

explain.code:
npm audit                      # report known CVEs in the tree
npm audit --omit=dev           # only what ships to production
npm audit fix                  # apply semver-compatible fixes
npm audit signatures           # verify registry signatures and provenance attestations

list: Triage: is the vulnerable function reachable from your code? A ReDoS in a dev-only CLI is not the same as one in your request parser.
If the fix is in a transitive dependency, use `overrides` to force the patched version until the parent package updates.
Automate updates with small, frequent PRs (Renovate, Dependabot), backed by good tests.

What happens
Defence
rows: Malicious package with a near-identical name
Review new deps, check download counts and repo
Real package publishes a malicious version
Lockfile, delay adopting brand-new versions, signatures/provenance
`postinstall` runs code on dev and CI machines
Public package with the name of your private one
Scoped packages (`@acme/...`) and a scoped registry in .npmrc

list: Fewer dependencies: a 5-line helper does not need a package.
Run the service as a non-root user in a minimal image; production installs with `--omit=dev`.
CI tokens with publish rights should be scoped, short-lived and protected by 2FA or trusted publishing.
Generate an SBOM (`npm sbom`) so you can answer "are we affected?" quickly when a new CVE appears.

explain.note: Node itself has a permission model (`--permission`, stable in Node 22.13+/23.5+) that can restrict file system, child process and worker access. It is a defence-in-depth layer, not a sandbox for untrusted code.

followups.q: npm audit reports 50 vulnerabilities. What do you do?
followups.a: Filter to production dependencies, sort by severity, check reachability and whether a fix exists. Fix critical, reachable ones first, use overrides for transitive fixes, and document accepted risks rather than ignoring the report.

followups.q: What does the integrity field protect against?
followups.a: It ensures the tarball you download is byte-for-byte the one recorded in the lockfile, so a tampered registry response or mirror is detected. It does not protect against a malicious version you locked in the first place.

mistakes: Running npm audit fix --force blindly, which can jump major versions and break the app.
Treating every audit warning as equally urgent.
Not committing the lockfile, which removes integrity checks.
